items.title: Finding Density Given Mass and Volume

sections.normalized_html: An ice cube has a mass of [MATH: 288] grams and a volume of [MATH: 360] cubic centimeters. What is the density, in grams per cubic centimeter, of the ice cube?
sections.readable_text: An ice cube has a mass of [MATH: 288] grams and a volume of [MATH: 360] cubic centimeters. What is the density, in grams per cubic centimeter, of the ice cube?

sections.normalized_html:
Density is defined as the ratio of mass to volume:

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{m}{V}]

In this problem,

  • the mass is [MATH: m = 288] grams, and

  • the volume is [MATH: V = 360] cubic centimeters.

Substituting these values into the formula, we get

[MATH: \rho = \frac{288}{360} = 0.8.]

Therefore, the density is [MATH: 0.8] grams per cubic centimeter.

items.title: Computing a Cube's Mass Given Density and Edge Length

sections.normalized_html: An aluminium cube has a density of [MATH: 800] kilograms per cubic meter, and each edge has a length of [MATH: 0.7] meters. What is the mass, in kilograms, of the cube?
sections.readable_text: An aluminium cube has a density of [MATH: 800] kilograms per cubic meter, and each edge has a length of [MATH: 0.7] meters. What is the mass, in kilograms, of the cube?

sections.normalized_html:
Density is defined as the ratio of mass to volume:

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{m}{V}]

Here, we want to find the mass [MATH: m{:}]

[MATH: m = \rho \cdot V]

Since the object is a cube, its volume is given by

[MATH: V = s^3,]

where [MATH: s] is the length of an edge.

In this problem,

  • the density is [MATH: \rho = 800 \ \text{kg/m}^3], and

  • the edge length is [MATH: s = 0.7 \ \text{m}.]

First, we evaluate the volume of the cube:
[MATH: V|= s^{3}; = (0.7)^{3}; = 0.343m^{3}]

Next, we find its mass of the cube:

[MATH: m|= ρ ⋅ V; = 800 ⋅ 0.343; = 274.4kg]

Therefore, the mass of the cube is [MATH: 274.4] kilograms.

items.title: Computing a Cube's Edge Length Given Mass and Density

sections.normalized_html: An iron cube has a mass of [MATH: 1{,}331] kilograms and a density of [MATH: 7{,}000] kilograms per cubic meter. What is the length of one edge of the cube, in meters? Round your final answer to the nearest hundredth of a meter.
sections.readable_text: An iron cube has a mass of [MATH: 1{,}331] kilograms and a density of [MATH: 7{,}000] kilograms per cubic meter. What is the length of one edge of the cube, in meters? Round your final answer to the nearest hundredth of a meter.

sections.normalized_html:
Density is defined as the ratio of mass to volume:

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{m}{V}]

We can use this formula to find the volume [MATH: V{:}]

[MATH: V = \dfrac{m}{\rho}]

In this problem,

  • the mass is [MATH: m = 1{,}331] kilograms, and

  • the density is [MATH: \rho = 7{,}000] kilograms per cubic meter.

Substituting these values, we get

[MATH: V|= (m)/(ρ); = (1,331)/(7,000); = 0.1901m^{3}.]

Since the object is a cube, its volume is given by

[MATH: V = s^3,]

where [MATH: s] is the length of an edge.

Thus, we have

[MATH: s|= root(V, 3); = root(0.1901, 3); ≈ 0.58m,]

rounded to the hundredth of a meter.

Therefore, the length of the edge of the cube is approximately [MATH: 0.58] meters.
